passages.t: Faith that grows, and love that increases, under pressure
passages.happening:
The letter opens like the first one: “Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy, To the church of the Thessalonians in God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: Grace and peace to you from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 1-2).

Then Paul gives thanks. “We are obligated to thank God for you all the time, brothers, as is fitting, because your faith is growing more and more, and your love for one another is increasing. That is why we boast among God’s churches about your perseverance and faith in the face of all the persecution and affliction you are enduring” (verses 3-4).
passages.hearers:
Some time has passed since the first letter, perhaps weeks or months. The church has kept its faith, but the persecution has not stopped. It may have grown.

Notice the words ‘obligated’ and ‘fitting’. Paul says thanks is owed to God for what he has done in these people. It is not flattery. It is giving God his due.

In the first letter Paul prayed that their love would ‘increase and overflow’ (1 Thessalonians 3:12). Now he says it is. And their faith is ‘growing more and more’. Paul's word means to grow beyond measure. Under pressure, this young church was not shrinking. It was growing.

The pressure came, as before, from their own neighbours. In a Greek city, turning from the gods could look like a danger to everyone, since the gods were thought to protect the city. And loyalty to ‘another king, named Jesus’ (Acts 17:7) could look like disloyalty to Caesar. This was probably not an order from Rome. It was the steady hostility of family, neighbours, trade partners and local officials.

And Paul boasts about them to other churches. A church that the world looked down on was being held up as an example.
passages.ot:
The growth of the righteous is a picture the Old Testament loves. “He is like a tree planted by streams of water, yielding its fruit in season, whose leaf does not wither” (Psalm 1:3). “The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon” (Psalm 92:12). And “The path of the righteous is like the first gleam of dawn, shining brighter and brighter until midday” (Proverbs 4:18).

Paul's boasting about them is the right kind of boasting, the kind Jeremiah described, in what God does: “let him who boasts boast in this, that he understands and knows Me” (Jeremiah 9:24).
passages.asks: Paul thanks God that faith and love were growing in a church under pressure. Ask whether hard times have made your faith grow or shrink. Ask whom you could thank God for, and tell. And ask whether your church is the kind others could hold up as an example of love for one another.

passages.t: God is just: relief for the afflicted when the Lord Jesus is revealed
passages.happening:
“All this is clear evidence of God’s righteous judgment. And so you will be counted worthy of the kingdom of God, for which you are suffering” (verse 5).

“After all, it is only right for God to repay with affliction those who afflict you, and to grant relief to you who are oppressed and to us as well. This will take place when the Lord Jesus is revealed from heaven with His mighty angels in blazing fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God and do not obey the gospel of our Lord Jesus” (verses 6-8).

“They will suffer the penalty of eternal destruction, separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might, on the day He comes to be glorified in His saints and regarded with wonder by all who have believed, including you who have believed our testimony” (verses 9-10).
passages.hearers:
This passage answers the question that suffering people ask: will God do anything? Paul says yes.

First, their endurance is itself a sign that God is at work and that his judgment is just. They are suffering ‘for’ the kingdom of God. Their pain has a cause, and it has a future.

Second, God will set things right. The ancient world had a strong sense that good should be repaid with good and harm with harm, and that a just ruler did this fairly. Paul says God will do it: affliction for those who afflict, and ‘relief’ for those who are oppressed. The word for relief means a loosening, the opposite of the pressing hardship Paul calls affliction.

Third, it will happen when the Lord Jesus is ‘revealed’. The word means unveiled. Jesus is Lord now, though the world does not see it. On that day it will be seen. ‘Blazing fire’ and ‘mighty angels’ are pictures of God's own coming from the Old Testament, and Paul uses them of Jesus.

Notice two things the believers are not told. They are not told to strike back. Vengeance belongs to God, not to them. And they are not told that judgment is something to enjoy. The passage ends not with the punishment of the wicked but with wonder: Christ ‘glorified in His saints and regarded with wonder by all who have believed’. That includes the Thessalonians, who believed when Paul preached to them.
passages.ot:
The pictures come from the prophets. “For behold, the LORD will come with fire” (Isaiah 66:15). Those who will be ‘separated from the presence of the Lord and the glory of His might’ echo Isaiah's refrain about people fleeing “from the terror of the LORD and from the splendor of His majesty” (Isaiah 2:19). In Isaiah these words speak of the LORD himself. Paul speaks them of the Lord Jesus.

Vengeance belongs to God: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay” (Deuteronomy 32:35). The psalmists cried out for it, “How long will the wicked, O LORD, how long will the wicked exult?” (Psalm 94:3), and left it with God: “Be still before the LORD and wait patiently for Him” (Psalm 37:7).

And Isaiah promised the persecuted faithful that God would vindicate them. Speaking of those who exclude them for God's name, he says, “But they will be put to shame” (Isaiah 66:5).
passages.hard:
These verses speak of vengeance and ‘eternal destruction’. How should they be read, and does this fit a God of love?

First, see who these words were for. They were written to comfort people who were being wronged, not to stir them to hatred. The Bible forbids personal revenge precisely because it leaves judgment to God: “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath” (Romans 12:19). A God who never judged would leave the persecuted without justice. And God takes no pleasure in anyone's ruin: “I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but rather that the wicked should turn from their ways and live” (Ezekiel 33:11).

Second, what all Christians confess. Every Christian tradition confesses that Christ will come again to judge the living and the dead, and that his judgment is just. The greatest loss in this passage is the loss of the Lord's presence.

Third, where Christians differ. Most of the church through history has read ‘eternal destruction’ as eternal, conscious separation from God's presence and glory. Others, holding the view called conditional immortality, read ‘destruction’ as a final end of existence, eternal in its effect. Both views take judgment seriously; they differ on its nature. These notes do not choose. The site's chapter note on 2 Thessalonians 1 and the doctrine study ‘Hell and Final Destinies’ set out the views, and the Honest Answer ‘Is hell forever, or does it end?’ goes further.

The judgment falls on those who ‘do not know God and do not obey the gospel’. That is the same gospel Paul begged everyone to receive. While there is time, the door is open.
passages.asks: Paul tells a suffering church that God is just, and that justice belongs to him. Ask whether you are holding on to a wrong done to you, hoping to pay it back yourself. Ask whether you believe God sees what others suffer, including people far from you. And ask whether, when you think of the Lord's coming, wonder is part of what you feel.

passages.t: A prayer to be worthy of the calling
passages.happening: “To this end, we always pray for you, that our God will count you worthy of His calling, and that He will powerfully fulfill your every good desire and work of faith, so that the name of our Lord Jesus will be glorified in you, and you in Him, according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ” (verses 11-12).
passages.hearers:
Paul turns from the future back to the present. Until the Lord comes, he prays.

‘Count you worthy of His calling’ does not mean earn your place. The word appears in verse 5 too. Worthiness here is a life that fits the calling God has already given, the way clothes fit the person they were made for. And notice who does the work: ‘He will powerfully fulfill’ every good desire and work of faith. The good they want to do, God gives them the power to do.

The goal is glory. In verse 10, Christ will be glorified in his saints on the last day. In verse 12, Paul prays that his name will be glorified in them now. And then the surprising words: ‘and you in Him’. Their honour is wrapped up in his. When the world looks down on them, they are being raised up in Christ.

The last words hold it all together: ‘according to the grace of our God and of the Lord Jesus Christ’. Grace comes from the Father and the Son together. Everything in the chapter, the endurance, the justice, the glory and the good works, rests on grace.
passages.ot:
God's people were made to show his glory: “You are My Servant, Israel, in whom I will display My glory” (Isaiah 49:3).

The right response to glory is to give it to God: “Not to us, O LORD, not to us, but to Your name be the glory” (Psalm 115:1).

And God's grace is what his people wait for: “Therefore the LORD longs to be gracious to you; therefore He rises to show you compassion, for the LORD is a just God” (Isaiah 30:18). The justice of verses 5 to 10 and the grace of verse 12 come from the same God.
passages.asks: Paul prays that God will fulfil every good desire his friends have. Ask what good thing you want to do but lack the strength for, and pray about it. Ask whether people who see your life see anything of Jesus. And ask whether you are trying to be worthy by your own effort, or by the grace of God.
